publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 6 On Sacred Scripture's clarity, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS mid-238–244): clarity defined so saving faith and manners can be surely known; catholic ASSERTIO that saving dogmas are plain; eleven reasons (Scripture's witness, lamp, Spirit's promise, command to search, Bereans, fathers, Scripture's end, God revealing, prophets/Apostles, revealed dogmas, style); partial obscurity admitted with six reasons God willed it; conditioned and sufficient perspicuity for those who read decently; Cap. 6 close that Scripture alone is God's certain and infallible testimony. Cap. 7 On Scripture's sense and interpretation begins PHYS 245; Cap. 5 complete; the rest of the Syntagma remains.
publication_scope.era_note: Crocius wrote in the early seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the illustrious school of Bremen. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1636 Villerian folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: CAPUT SEXTUM. De sacrae Scripturae claritate. Haec de sacrae Scripturae perfectione & sufficientia: sequitur claritas, quae est illius proprietas, qua in ea ita aperte posita sunt et inveniuntur illa omnia, quae continent fidem moresque vivendi, ut adhibitis cum debita diligentia & prudentia mediis convenientibus per DEI auxilium a DEI timentibus nihilque sibi, suoque carnali judicio tribuentibus pro cujusque aetate certo sciri & ad salutem intelligi possint.
english:
CHAPTER SIX
On Sacred Scripture's clarity

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's perfection and sufficiency: next comes clarity. Clarity is Scripture's property by which everything that holds the faith and the manners of living is so openly set down in it, and so found there, that God-fearers — using fitting means with due diligence and prudence, helped by God, and attributing nothing to themselves or to their fleshly judgment — can, for each person's age, know it surely and understand it unto salvation.

source_text: Obscuritates igitur, si quae inesse videntur, adhibitis mediis, sunt vincibiles pio & cauto lectori. Recte enim Franciscus Lamberti, olim professor Marpurgensis, sacram scripturam docet eis patefieri, qui nihil sibi tribuunt, & suo judicio. Item, si possides ingenium, doctrinam, experientiam, his abrenuncia, cum accedis ad Christi scholam. Abrenuncia, inquam, non ut omnino illa nolis, sed ut nihil eis fidas: alioqui non eris idoneus Christi discipulus, & non docebit te, nec scripturarum desideratissimum ostium referabit. Veritatis enim & voluntatis DEI sola scriptura certum & infallibile testimonium est.
english: Obscurities, therefore, if any seem to be present, are conquerable when the means are applied, for the pious and cautious reader.

Rightly Francis Lambert, once professor at Marburg, teaches that Sacred Scripture is opened to those who attribute nothing to themselves and to their own judgment. Likewise: if you possess wit, learning, and experience, renounce these when you come to Christ's school. Renounce them, I say — not that you wholly refuse them, but that you trust nothing to them: otherwise you will not be a fit disciple of Christ, and he will neither teach you nor open Scripture's most longed-for door.
For of God's truth and will Scripture alone is the certain and infallible testimony.

source_text: Nos igitur hujus assertionis rationes aliquot distincte proponimus. 1. Quia Deus voluit, ut esset, cur cum Davide diceremus: Da mihi intellectum & scrutabor legem tuam, psal. 119. v.34. 2. Ut retunderetur arrogantia humana. 3. Ut removeretur fastidium. 4. Ut diligentia nostra excitaretur. 5. Ut ipsa sacra scriptura in majori pretio haberetur, id quod Theodoretus praefatione in Ezechielem variis exemplis declarat. 6. Ut desiderium vehementius vitae alterius in nobis accenderetur, ubi non amplius ex parte cognoscemus, & ex parte prophetabimus, sed quod imperfectum est, tolletur, & cernemus coram, non per speculum aut per aenigma, 1. Cor. 13.v.9. & seqq. Consule Flacium Illyricum in clavis parte altera tract. 1. de ratione cognoscendi sacras literas. Scite Augustinus verbis supra allegatis subnectit: Nihil fere de illis obscuritatibus eruitur, quod non alibi clarissime dictum reperiatur. Ante omnia igitur opus est Dei timore converti ad cognoscendam ejus voluntatem. Et lib. eodem c.9. Ad obscuriores locutiones illustrandas de manifestioribus sumantur exempla & certarum sententiarum testimonia dubitationem de incertis auferant. Huc etiam facit lex Constantini Magni apud Theodoretum lib. 1. hist. Eccl. lata suffragantibus trecentis & octodecim episcopis in concilio Niceno: Εὐαγγελικαὶ καὶ ἀποστολικαὶ βίβλοι καὶ τῶν παλαιῶν προφητῶν τὰ θεσπίσματα σαφῶς ἡμᾶς ἐκπαιδεύουσι τὸ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ φρονεῖν. τὴν τοίνυν πολεμικὴν ἀποθέμενοι ἔριν ἐκ τῶν θεοπνεύστων λογίων λάβωμεν τῶν ζητουμένων τὴν λύσιν. Euangelici & Apostolici libri & antiquorum prophetarum oracula perspicue nos instruunt sensu numinis, hoc est, quid de Deo rebusque divinis nos sentire oporteat. Igitur hostili deposita discordia sumamus ex scripturis divinitus inspiratis solutionem decisionemque controversiarum, de quibus agendum est.
english: We therefore distinctly set out several reasons for this assertion.
1. Because God willed that there should be cause to say with David: "Give me understanding, and I will search your law" ([[Psalm 119:34 >> Bible:Psalm 119:34]]).
2. That human arrogance might be beaten back.
3. That distaste might be removed.
4. That our diligence might be stirred.
5. That Sacred Scripture itself might be held in greater price — which Theodoret in the preface to Ezekiel declares by various examples.

6. That a keener desire for the other life might be kindled in us, where we will no longer know in part and prophesy in part, but what is imperfect will be done away, and we will see face to face, not through a mirror or in a riddle ([[1 Corinthians 13:9 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:9]] and following).

Consult Flacius Illyricus, Clavis part 2 treatise 1 on the way of knowing the sacred letters. Wisely Augustine adds to the words cited above: "Almost nothing is drawn from those obscurities that is not found said most clearly elsewhere." Before all things, therefore, one must be turned by the fear of God to knowing his will. And in the same book chapter 9: to illustrate obscurer locutions, examples are to be taken from the clearer ones, and the testimonies of certain sentences are to remove doubt about the uncertain.

Here also belongs the law of Constantine the Great in Theodoret (Church History book 1), passed with the votes of three hundred eighteen bishops in the Nicene council: the Evangelical and Apostolic books and the oracles of the ancient prophets perspicuously instruct us in the sense of the Deity — that is, what we ought to think about God and divine things. Therefore, hostile discord laid aside, let us take from the divinely inspired Scriptures the solution and decision of the controversies that are to be handled.

source_text: II. DEINDE non negamus sacram scripturam aliqua ex parte alicubi & alicui obscuram esse, sive res sublimes & mysteriorum plenas, sive phrases antiqui illius temporis proprias, tropicas item figuratasque spectemus locutiones, quae hoc tempore nobis difficultatem aliquam pariant. Quam obscuritatem augent hominum praejudicia, linguarum & rerum ignorantia, vana confidentia, negligentia, odium, invidia, ambitio, avaritia, altercandi libido, omnisque pravus affectus, quo mens excaecatur. Hinc & Petrus epist. 2. cap.3.v.16. de epistolis Paulinis affirmat, quod δυσνόητά τινα contineant, ad domandam labore superbiam, & intellectum a fastidio removendum, cui facile investigata plerunque vilescunt. Nam magnifice & salubriter Spiritus sanctus ita scripturas modificavit, ut locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus fastidia detergeret, ut sapienter scribit Augustinus lib. 2. de doctrina Christiana cap. 6.
english: II. Next, we do not deny that Sacred Scripture is in some part, somewhere, and for someone obscure — whether we look at sublime matters full of mysteries, or at phrases proper to that ancient time, and also tropic and figured locutions that in this age make some difficulty for us.

That obscurity is increased by human prejudices, ignorance of tongues and of things, vain confidence, negligence, hatred, envy, ambition, avarice, lust of wrangling, and every depraved affection by which the mind is blinded.

Hence Peter also ([[2 Peter 3:16 >> Bible:2 Peter 3:16]]), concerning Paul's letters, affirms that they contain some things hard to understand (δυσνόητά τινα) — to tame pride by labor, and to remove the intellect from distaste, for what is easily investigated often becomes cheap to it.

For magnificently and wholesomely the Holy Spirit so shaped the Scriptures that by the clearer places he meets hunger, and by the obscurer ones he wipes away distaste — as Augustine wisely writes (On Christian Doctrine book 2 chapter 6).

source_text: III. Non igitur absolutam & omnimodam perspicuitatem scripturarum, ad nos relatarum, asserimus, sed conditionatam & sufficientem ad canonicum & didacticum officium praestandum iis, qui eas decenter legunt & scrutantur. Hoc demonstratur ex Joh. 5.39. & psal. 19.12. Εἰσὶν γὰρ ἐνταῦθα πάντα ἀναγκαῖα, σαφῆ, εὐθέα — omnia necessaria, clara, manifesta & recta, teste Chrysostomo tom. 3. in 2. ad Thess. οὐ μόνον ἀσαφείας, neque indiga explicationis, sed duntaxat auditionis, teste Justino Martyre dialogo cum Tryphone: tamen diligenti scrutinio & meditatione opus est, ut lectori perspicua evadant, juxta Cyrillum Alexandrinum lib. 9. contra Julianum: Nihil, dicentem, est difficile iis, qui in scripturis versantur, ut decet. Et Clementem Alexand. l.7. Strom. Δεῖ τὰς γραφὰς ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάζειν, οὐ παρέργως ἀναγινώσκειν — oportet scripturas accurate perscrutari, non obiter legere. Et Epiphanium haeres.: πάντα σαφῆ ἐν τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ τοῖς βουλομένοις εὐσεβεῖ λογισμῷ προσέρχεσθαι τῷ θείῳ λόγῳ — omnia clara in divina scriptura volentibus pio ratiocinio accedere divino sermoni.
english: III. We therefore do not assert an absolute and every-way perspicuity of the Scriptures handed down to us, but a conditioned and sufficient one for discharging the canonical and didactic office for those who read and search them decently.

This is shown from [[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]] and [[Psalm 19:12 >> Bible:Psalm 19:12]]. For here are all things needful, clear, and straight — all necessary, clear, manifest, and right — Chrysostom witnessing (volume 3 on 2 Thessalonians); not needing explanation but only hearing — Justin Martyr witnessing (Dialogue with Trypho). Yet diligent scrutiny and meditation are needed so that they become perspicuous to the reader, according to Cyril of Alexandria (Against Julian book 9): "Nothing is hard for those who dwell in the Scriptures as they ought." And Clement of Alexandria (Stromata book 7): one must examine the Scriptures accurately, not read them casually. And Epiphanius (Against heresies): all things are clear in the divine Scripture for those who wish to approach the divine word with pious reasoning.
